snip.t: Rheumatic Diseases: Conditions like rheumatoid arthritis can cause vasculitis.
Rheumatic diseases: Can be associated with increased susceptibility to certain infections due to underlying immune dysregulation or treatment.
Rheumatic diseases: Systemic Lupus Erythematosus (SLE) can cause lupus nephritis, an autoimmune glomerulonephritis.
Symptoms of underlying cause: Fever (infection), joint pain (rheumatic disease), easy bruising (vasculitis).
Rheumatic diseases (e.g., lupus): Vasculitic skin lesions prone to infection — Immunosuppressive therapy

Comorbidities: HIV status, diabetes, sickle‑cell disease, peripheral vascular disease, chronic steroid use, recent TB treatment, malaria, rheumatic disease — Immunocompromise or vascular disease predisposes to atypical organisms and poorer outcomes
Other comorbidities: Sickle cell disease (vascular compromise), rheumatic diseases (e.g., ankylosing spondylitis)
Sickle cell / rheumatic disease: “Do you have sickle cell disease or a history of rheumatic fever?” — Sickle cell nephropathy or immune‑complex GN can present similarly.

qs.q: What is the maximum age limit for the onset of joint symptoms to classify a childhood rheumatic disease as juvenile idiopathic arthritis?
qs.e: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is a broad term for childhood rheumatic diseases that begin before the age of 16 and are characterized by joint inflammation lasting more than 6 weeks. It was formerly called juvenile rheumatoid arthritis.

qs.q: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis is defined as a broad term for childhood rheumatic diseases that begin before a specific age and are characterized by joint inflammation lasting longer than what duration?
qs.e: Juvenile idiopathic arthritis includes childhood rheumatic diseases that begin before the age of 16 and are characterized by joint inflammation that lasts more than 6 weeks. It was formerly called juvenile rheumatoid arthritis.

qs.q: Decreased values in conjunction with pleural fluid/blood glucose ratios <1.0 may occur in effusions due to underlying bacterial, tuberculous, malignant, and rheumatic disease.
qs.e: A low pleural fluid glucose level (and a low pleural fluid/serum glucose ratio <1.0) is characteristic of exudative effusions caused by increased glucose utilization by inflammatory cells (bacteria, malignant cells) or impaired glucose transport into the pleural space. This is commonly seen in bacterial pneumonia, empyema, tuberculous pleuritis, and malignant effusions.

ai.subject: Medicine
ai.summary: Rheumatic diseases encompass autoimmune, inflammatory, and infectious conditions that affect joints, heart, and skin. In East Africa, rheumatic fever and tuberculosis‑associated arthritis are common. Clinical reasoning focuses on history, exam, and pragmatic investigations.

sections.p: Rheumatic disease refers to any condition where the immune system or infection damages musculoskeletal or cardiovascular tissues. Diagnosis combines clinical criteria, serology, imaging, and response to therapy.
b: Use ACR/EULAR criteria for RA; Jones criteria for rheumatic fever; 2019 SLE classification; TB arthritis requires culture or PCR

t.b: Inflammatory activity – high levels suggest active disease
Positive in RA – supports diagnosis but not exclusive
Positive in SLE – indicates systemic involvement
Suggests ankylosing spondylitis or reactive arthritis
Screen for latent TB before immunosuppression
Excludes septic arthritis – look for crystals, WBC count

sections.p: Severity is graded by functional status and organ involvement. Use DAS28 for RA, WHO staging for TB, and SLEDAI for lupus.
In low‑resource areas, infections dominate. HIV, TB, malaria, schistosomiasis, and rheumatic fever are top culprits, followed by genetic autoimmune diseases.
Patients present with joint pain, swelling, morning stiffness, fever, and systemic signs. Cardiac murmurs, skin rashes, and renal dysfunction may accompany systemic disease.
Prioritise tests that are affordable and available. Use clinical scoring when labs are missing.

t.b: Rule out septic arthritis – positive culture = infection
Detect erosions in RA or calcifications in TB arthritis
Assess valvular lesions in rheumatic fever

sections.p: Urgent signs include rapidly progressive heart failure, severe pain with fever, haemoptysis, or neurological deficits. Complications: heart failure, renal failure, septic shock.
b: Uncontrolled fever >38.5°C with joint swelling – suspect septic arthritis

sections.p: Treat the underlying cause first, then control inflammation. Use drugs that are affordable and have a favourable safety profile.
b: Hydroxychloroquine for mild RA and SLE – inexpensive

t.b: Rapid control of inflammation – avoid if active TB or uncontrolled diabetes
Alternative to MTX when MTX unavailable – monitor liver function

sections.p: Regular monitoring of disease activity, drug toxicity, and comorbidities. Vaccinate against pneumococcus and influenza; counsel on smoking cessation.
Infections such as septic arthritis, gout, and malaria can mimic rheumatic disease.
Seronegative RA may have negative RF/anti‑CCP. TB arthritis may show normal CRP. HIV serology can be false‑negative early.
b: Low CRP in TB arthritis – rely on imaging

whenToSeekHelp: Rapidly worsening dyspnoea with new murmur

faq.q: Why is NSAID preferred first line in low‑resource settings?
faq.a: They control pain, are cheap, and have a known safety profile.

faq.q: What if a patient has both HIV and RA?
faq.a: Start antiretroviral therapy first, then consider hydroxychloroquine; avoid MTX until viral load is suppressed.

faq.q: How to differentiate TB arthritis from RA when imaging is limited?
faq.a: Look for cold abscesses, sinus tracts, and a history of TB exposure; synovial fluid culture is definitive.

exam: A 28‑year‑old woman presents with polyarthritis and a malar rash. What is the next best test? — ANA; positive supports SLE diagnosis.
A patient with chronic joint pain improves on NSAIDs but develops a new heart murmur. What is the likely diagnosis? — Rheumatic fever; look for ASO titre.
You have a patient with fever and monoarthritis. Synovial fluid is turbid but cultures are pending. What is the immediate management? — Start empiric antibiotics for septic arthritis.
A 45‑year‑old man with HIV on ART develops swelling of the knee. What is the most likely cause? — TB arthritis; order X‑ray and GeneXpert.
Why is prednisone avoided in a patient with active TB? — It suppresses immunity and worsens infection.
A child has a history of rheumatic fever and now has a new systolic murmur. What is the most appropriate investigation? — Echocardiography to assess valvular damage.
A patient with RA is on hydroxychloroquine but develops visual disturbances. What is the action? — Stop the drug and refer for ophthalmology.
You suspect vasculitis in a patient with rash and renal dysfunction. What test confirms it? — ANA and anti‑dsDNA; positive suggests lupus nephritis.
